```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(tidyverse)
library(broom)
```

## Introduction & Dataset

In this micro-report, we implement the tidy PCA workflow demonstrated by Claus O. Wilke. We use the standard `iris` morphological dataset (150 observations across 3 flower species: *setosa*, *versicolor*, and *virginica*) to illustrate scaling, principal component extraction, variance explained, and loading interpretation.

```{r}
#| label: load-data

iris_clean <- iris |>
  as_tibble()

head(iris_clean)
```

## Running PCA

Principal Component Analysis requires numeric variables. We scale features to unit variance so that differing measurement units do not skew the variance structure.

```{r}
#| label: run-pca

pca_fit <- iris_clean |>
  select(where(is.numeric)) |>
  prcomp(scale. = TRUE)

summary(pca_fit)
```

## Visualizing Principal Components (Score Plot)

Using `broom::augment()`, we join the projected PC coordinates back with the metadata (`Species`).

```{r}
#| label: plot-pca
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4

pca_augmented <- pca_fit |>
  augment(iris_clean)

ggplot(pca_augmented, aes(x = .fittedPC1, y = .fittedPC2, color = Species)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  labs(
    title = "PCA Score Plot of Iris Species",
    x = "Principal Component 1",
    y = "Principal Component 2"
  )
```

*Observation:* PC1 cleanly distinguishes *Iris setosa* from *versicolor* and *virginica*, while PC2 separates *versicolor* from *virginica*.

## Variance Explained (Scree Plot)

We extract eigenvalues using `broom::tidy(..., matrix = "eigenvalues")` to assess the proportion of variance captured.

```{r}
#| label: plot-variance
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.5

var_explained <- pca_fit |>
  tidy(matrix = "eigenvalues")

ggplot(var_explained, aes(x = PC, y = percent)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:4) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  labs(
    title = "Variance Explained per Principal Component",
    x = "Principal Component",
    y = "Percentage of Variance"
  )
```

PC1 accounts for ~73% of the variance, and PC1 + PC2 together account for over 95% of the total dataset variance.

## Feature Loadings (Rotation Matrix)

We inspect the rotation matrix via `broom::tidy(..., matrix = "rotation")` to observe which morphological traits drive each axis.

```{r}
#| label: plot-loadings
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4

loadings <- pca_fit |>
  tidy(matrix = "rotation")

ggplot(loadings, aes(x = value, y = column, fill = column)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(vars(PC), scales = "free_x") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  labs(
    title = "Variable Loadings across Principal Components",
    x = "Loading Weight",
    y = "Feature"
  )
```

Petal length and petal width exhibit large positive weights along PC1, explaining why species with larger petals cluster toward positive PC1 coordinates.

## Summary

Combining `prcomp()` with `broom::tidy()` and `broom::augment()` creates a clean, readable pipeline that fits directly into the tidyverse ecosystem without manual matrix slicing.
